title: Isandro and the Weather
premise: After her mother's funeral, Silas Thornbury returns to the family house to catalog its contents for sale, armed with a smile that ends conversations and a childhood of unanswered questions. When a radio plays an unrecorded song her mother once hummed in private, Silas discovers her mother had another life: a collaborator, Isandro Vey, whose letters and photographs were hidden behind the piano. As the closing date on the house looms, Silas traces Isandro through memory and rumor, learning that her mother's silence protected a betrayal — and that forgiveness may require giving up the inheritance itself. The novel ends with Silas signing the house over to Isandro's estranged daughter, walking out with only the song, finally sung aloud.
about_author: Vesper Okafor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's unfinished correspondence before turning to fiction. They write about inheritances — of houses, of guilt, of songs — from a coastal town where the weather changes faster than anyone can apologize.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Silas Thornbury, POV. Three days after the funeral, Silas begins cataloging her mother Edith's house room by room for the estate sale, practicing her professional smile on the realtor. She finds nothing personal anywhere — no letters, no photographs of Edith young. Emotional beat: controlled grief curdling into suspicion that she never knew this woman at all.

chapters.title: A Song With No Name
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Driving back from the lawyer's office, a radio station plays an unfamiliar melody that stops her at a red light: it is the tune Edith hummed while cooking, the one she claimed was hers alone. The DJ says it was submitted by a local man named Isandro Vey, 'written fifty years ago, never recorded until now.' Emotional beat: vertigo — the private made public.

chapters.title: Behind the Piano
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She tears apart the music room and finds a loose panel concealing a tin box: photographs of a young Edith laughing with a dark-haired stranger, and unsent letters addressed to 'I.' The house sale contract sits unsigned on the kitchen table. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery shadowed by the sense of trespassing into her mother's guarded heart.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Silas, POV, with interpolated fragments of Edith's letters. Reading the letters chronologically, Silas watches two young musicians plan a life together — then watch the letters stop mid-sentence, mid-plan. The last one is torn in half. Emotional beat: falling in love with a version of her mother she was never allowed to meet.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Kept
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She canvasses the aging neighborhood; Mrs. Okonkwo next door remembers 'the boy with the guitar' and goes quiet when Silas mentions his name. A neighbor warns her: some things Edith buried were buried for reasons. Emotional beat: first resistance — the town itself is complicit in the silence.

chapters.title: Isandro
chapters.summary: Isandro Vey, POV, 1971. Flashback: a hot summer of writing songs in Edith's garage, two voices braiding together, plans to leave for the city. His older brother Marcus mocks his seriousness; Edith's father forbids the door. Emotional beat: radiant, doomed hope rendered in present-tense warmth.

chapters.title: The Radio Man
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She tracks down the DJ, who reveals Isandro mailed the tape anonymously three weeks before Edith died — postmarked from a town two hours away. He is alive. The DJ plays her the B-side: a second song, angrier, with lyrics about a stolen credit. Emotional beat: hope sharpening into dread about what her mother did.

chapters.title: Stolen Credit
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV, 1972. Flashback: a producer offers to record their songs but only under Edith's father's terms — Isandro's name struck from the paperwork. Marcus urges him to sign anyway; Isandro refuses. Edith wavers between them. Emotional beat: the first crack — love tested against pride and survival.

chapters.title: The Unsigned Contract
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. The realtor pressures her to close; a developer's offer is generous and time-limited. Silas stalls, lying that she needs another week, and realizes she is now keeping secrets of her own — from her brother Dale, who wants the money and suspects nothing. Emotional beat: becoming her mother, one concealment at a time.

chapters.title: Dale's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Dale Thornbury, POV. Dale arrives to push the sale, all spreadsheets and grief converted to logistics. He finds the tin box open and accuses Silas of manufacturing drama to delay money he needs for his daughter's surgery consult. Emotional beat: sibling rupture — both grieving, neither able to say so.

chapters.title: The Half Letter
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Matching the torn letter against the box's lining, Silas reconstructs it: Edith confessing she signed the papers, took the credit, and let Isandro be erased — because her father threatened to disown her, and because she was afraid. The letter was never sent. Emotional beat: shame inherited like furniture.

chapters.title: Two Hours Away
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She drives to the postmark town and finds a shuttered guitar shop with Isandro's name still on the faded awning. A teenager sweeping the porch says the old man lives above it but 'doesn't take visitors, especially not reporters.' Emotional beat: the long approach — courage gathering at a locked door.

chapters.title: The Door That Doesn't Open
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She knocks; Isandro speaks through the door and refuses her — not angrily, but with terrible finality: 'Your mother had fifty years. I'm not spending my last ones on her ghost.' Silas leaves the half letter in his mailbox. Emotional beat: rejection that feels earned.

chapters.title: Marcus Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. She finds Marcus Vey, now a deacon, who tells a competing story: Isandro wasn't robbed, he was offered everything and chose pride over Edith, choosing the road over the woman. 'Ask yourself who abandoned whom.' Emotional beat: the ground shifting — memory as contested territory.

chapters.title: Edith's Tape
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Searching the attic, Silas finds a reel-to-reel labeled in Edith's hand: a recording of the two of them singing together, made the summer before everything broke. Listening, she hears the moment the harmony falters — an argument caught on tape, Edith saying 'I can't lose everything for a song.' Emotional beat: hearing her mother choose fear in real time.

chapters.title: The Developer's Deadline
chapters.summary: Dale, POV. Dale signs preliminary papers without Silas, forcing the issue; the closing is set for Friday. Confronted, he breaks: the medical bills are worse than he said, and his anger was terror wearing a suit. Emotional beat: pity displacing fury — the family's real poverty exposed.

chapters.title: Weather Coming In
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV, present day. Isandro has listened to the half letter forty times. His granddaughter Lila, estranged from him by his own stubbornness, arrives to check on him before a storm. He asks her to drive him somewhere and won't say where. Emotional beat: pride beginning, at last, to thaw.

chapters.title: The Garage
chapters.summary: Silas and Isandro, alternating POV. Isandro comes to the house during the storm's edge and stands in the ruined garage where they wrote the songs. He and Silas speak plainly for the first time — he tells her what her mother cost him; she tells him what her mother's silence cost her. Neither forgives yet. Emotional beat: truth spoken without absolution.

chapters.title: What Justice Looks Like Here
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas realizes no court, no contract, no apology restores anything — the only justice available is redistribution: the house, the royalties Edith quietly collected for decades, the name on the songs. She calls the lawyer and rewrites the estate. Dale, shown the tape, agrees — slowly. Emotional beat: justice as choice, not verdict.

chapters.title: Friday
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. At the closing, Silas signs the house and the song rights to Isandro and his granddaughter Lila; Dale takes the liquid share and shakes Isandro's hand awkwardly. Isandro, given the deed, looks smaller and lighter at once. Emotional beat: climax as quiet ceremony rather than confrontation.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Packing the last box, Silas writes a letter to Edith she will never send — not absolving her, but understanding her: afraid, small, loving in the only way she could. She leaves it in the empty music room for whoever comes next. Emotional beat: grief finally allowed to be ordinary.

chapters.title: The Song, Sung Aloud
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Weeks later, at Lila's invitation, Silas attends a small concert where Isandro performs the song with its true history told from the stage. He dedicates it 'to Edith, and to the child she raised better than she believed.' Silas sings along, badly, smiling a smile that starts conversations. Emotional beat: resolution — memory restored, inheritance transformed into voice.
